questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que el programa imprima `Python`.

```python
nombre = ___
print(nombre)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the program prints `Python`.

```python
nombre = ___
print(nombre)
```
questions.explanation_es: Cualquier expresión que evalúe al string `"Python"` sirve: el literal `"Python"`, `"Py" + "thon"`, `str.upper("python").capitalize()`... Python es de tipado dinámico: el nombre `nombre` simplemente se enlaza al objeto que resulte de evaluar la expresión.
questions.explanation_en: Any expression that evaluates to the string `"Python"` works: the literal `"Python"`, `"Py" + "thon"`, etc. Python is dynamically typed: the name `nombre` is simply bound to whatever object the right-hand expression evaluates to.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.question_es:

```python
print(x)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the program prints `3.5`.

```python
x = 7 / ___
print(x)
```
questions.explanation_es: El operador `/` siempre devuelve un `float` en Python 3, incluso si el resultado es un número entero (división real, distinta de `//`). `7 / 2` da `3.5`. Cualquier divisor que produzca ese cociente es válido.
questions.explanation_en: The `/` operator always returns a `float` in Python 3, even when the result is a whole number (true division, unlike `//`). `7 / 2` gives `3.5`. Any divisor producing that quotient is valid.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Expressions: Binary arithmetic operations

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que el programa imprima `10` (como entero, no como texto).

```python
texto = "010"
numero = ___(texto)
print(numero + 0)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the program prints `10` (as an integer, not text).

```python
texto = "010"
numero = ___(texto)
print(numero + 0)
```
questions.explanation_es: `int("010")` convierte (hace *casting*) el string `"010"` al entero `10`; el cero a la izquierda no molesta a `int()`. Sumarle `0` no cambia el valor pero confirma que es numérico: si `numero` siguiera siendo un string, `numero + 0` lanzaría `TypeError`. `int()` lanza `ValueError` si el texto no representa un entero válido. `eval("010")` no sirve aquí aunque suene parecido: Python 3 prohíbe los ceros a la izquierda en literales enteros decimales, así que `eval` lanza `SyntaxError` en vez de devolver `10` — la razón por la que este ejercicio usa `"010"` y no `"10"`, donde ambas funciones habrían coincidido por casualidad.
questions.explanation_en: `int("010")` converts (casts) the string `"010"` to the integer `10`; the leading zero doesn't bother `int()`. Adding `0` doesn't change the value but confirms it's numeric: if `numero` were still a string, `numero + 0` would raise `TypeError`. `int()` raises `ValueError` when the text isn't a valid integer. `eval("010")` won't work here even though it sounds similar: Python 3 forbids leading zeros in decimal integer literals, so `eval` raises `SyntaxError` instead of returning `10` — the reason this exercise uses `"010"` instead of `"10"`, where both functions would have coincidentally matched.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Built-in Functions: int()

```python
n = 8
```

questions.explanation_es: `n % 2` es el resto de dividir `n` entre 2: vale `0` cuando `n` es par. La condición `n % 2 == 0` es la forma estándar de comprobar paridad en Python.

questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Expressions: Binary arithmetic operations (modulo)

```python
for i in range(5):

print(total)
```

questions.explanation_es: `total += i` es azúcar sintáctico para `total = total + i`: acumula `i` en `total` en cada vuelta del bucle. Tras iterar `range(5)` (0,1,2,3,4), `total` vale `10`.

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que el bucle imprima `0`, `1` y `2` y luego pare (sin imprimir `3`).

```python
n = 0
while n ___ 3:
    print(n)
    n += 1
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the loop prints `0`, `1`, `2` and then stops (without printing `3`).

```python
n = 0
while n ___ 3:
    print(n)
    n += 1
```
questions.explanation_es: `while n < 3` mantiene el bucle mientras `n` sea menor que 3: se ejecuta con `n = 0, 1, 2` (imprimiéndolos) y se detiene cuando `n` llega a `3`, porque la condición se evalúa *antes* de cada iteración.
questions.explanation_en: `while n < 3` keeps looping while `n` is less than 3: it runs with `n = 0, 1, 2` (printing them) and stops once `n` reaches `3`, because the condition is checked *before* each iteration.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Compound statements: The while statement

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que la lista resultante sea `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]` (los pares del 0 al 9).

```python
pares = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 ___ 0]
print(pares)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the resulting list is `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]` (the even numbers from 0 to 9).

```python
pares = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 ___ 0]
print(pares)
```
questions.explanation_es: Una comprensión de listas `[expr for var in iterable if condicion]` filtra los elementos que cumplen `condicion`. `x % 2 == 0` es verdadero solo para los pares, así que el resultado es `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]`.
questions.explanation_en: A list comprehension `[expr for var in iterable if condition]` keeps only elements matching `condition`. `x % 2 == 0` is true only for even numbers, so the result is `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Data structures: List Comprehensions

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que la lista resultante sea `[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]` (los cuadrados del 1 al 5).

```python
print(cuadrados)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the resulting list is `[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]` (the squares from 1 to 5).

```python
cuadrados = [___ for n in range(1, 6)]
print(cuadrados)
```
questions.explanation_es: La parte antes de `for` en una comprensión es la expresión que se evalúa para cada elemento. `n ** 2` (o `n * n`) eleva cada número del rango `1..5` al cuadrado, dando `[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]`.
questions.explanation_en: The part before `for` in a comprehension is the expression evaluated for each element. `n ** 2` (or `n * n`) squares each number in `1..5`, giving `[1, 4, 9, 16, 25]`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Data structures: List Comprehensions

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que `potencia(2, 3)` imprima `8` usando un valor por defecto para el exponente.

```python
def potencia(base, exponente=___):
    return base ** exponente

print(potencia(2, 3))
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so `potencia(2, 3)` prints `8`, using a default value for the exponent.

```python
def potencia(base, exponente=___):
    return base ** exponente

print(potencia(2, 3))
```
questions.explanation_es: El valor por defecto (`exponente=2`, por ejemplo) solo se usa si el llamador no pasa ese argumento; aquí `potencia(2, 3)` sí lo pasa explícitamente (`3`), así que el resultado es `2 ** 3 = 8` sin importar qué default se puso, siempre que sea un número válido.
questions.explanation_en: The default value (e.g. `exponente=2`) only applies when the caller omits that argument; here `potencia(2, 3)` passes it explicitly (`3`), so the result is `2 ** 3 = 8` regardless of the default, as long as it's a valid number.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Compound statements: Function definitions (default argument values)

questions.explanation_es: `*numeros` empaqueta todos los argumentos posicionales en una tupla llamada `numeros`. `sum()` suma sus elementos: `1+2+3+4 = 10`. Sin `*args` la función solo aceptaría un número fijo de argumentos.
questions.explanation_en: `*numeros` packs every positional argument into a tuple named `numeros`. `sum()` adds its elements: `1+2+3+4 = 10`. Without `*args` the function could only accept a fixed number of arguments.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Compound statements: Function definitions (*args)

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que el programa imprima `10` y luego `5` (la variable global no cambia dentro de la función sin `global`).

```python
x = 5

def modifica():
    x = ___
    print(x)

modifica()
print(x)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the program prints `10` and then `5` (the global variable is unchanged inside the function without `global`).

```python
x = 5

def modifica():
    x = ___
    print(x)

modifica()
print(x)
```
questions.explanation_es: Dentro de `modifica`, `x = 10` crea una variable *local* llamada `x` que oculta (sombrea) a la global durante la función; por eso se imprime `10`. Al terminar la función, la `x` global de fuera sigue valiendo `5`. Para modificar la global de verdad haría falta la palabra clave `global x`.
questions.explanation_en: Inside `modifica`, `x = 10` creates a *local* variable named `x` that shadows the global one for the duration of the function — that's why `10` is printed. Once the function returns, the outer global `x` is still `5`. Actually mutating the global would require the `global x` keyword.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — The Python Language Reference: Execution model (naming and binding) — https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html#naming-and-binding

questions.explanation_es: Una `lambda` es una función anónima de una sola expresión: `lambda n: n ** 2` es equivalente a `def cuadrado(n): return n ** 2`. No puede contener sentencias, solo una expresión que se devuelve implícitamente.

questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Expressions: Lambdas

```python
pares = [(1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 3)]
pares.sort(key=___)
print(pares)
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so the list ends up sorted by the second element of each tuple: `[(2, 1), (1, 2), (3, 3)]`.

```python

pares.sort(key=___)
print(pares)
```
questions.explanation_es: `key=lambda p: p[1]` le dice a `sort()` que ordene usando el segundo elemento de cada tupla (`p[1]`) en vez del valor completo de la tupla. El orden resultante por segundo elemento (1, 2, 3) es `[(2, 1), (1, 2), (3, 3)]`. `list.sort()` es estable e in-place.
questions.explanation_en: `key=lambda p: p[1]` tells `sort()` to order using each tuple's second element (`p[1]`) instead of the whole tuple. Sorted by second element (1, 2, 3) the result is `[(2, 1), (1, 2), (3, 3)]`. `list.sort()` is stable and in-place.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Sorting HOW TO

questions.question_es:
Completa el hueco para que `factorial(4)` imprima `24` usando recursión.

```python
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * ___

print(factorial(4))
```
questions.question_en:
Fill in the blank so `factorial(4)` prints `24`, using recursion.

```python
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * ___

print(factorial(4))
```
questions.explanation_es: El caso recursivo multiplica `n` por el factorial de `n - 1`: `factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1)`. El caso base (`n <= 1`) detiene la recursión devolviendo `1`. `factorial(4) = 4*3*2*1 = 24`.
questions.explanation_en: The recursive case multiplies `n` by the factorial of `n - 1`: `factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1)`. The base case (`n <= 1`) stops the recursion by returning `1`. `factorial(4) = 4*3*2*1 = 24`.
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Compound statements: Function definitions (recursive calls)

questions.explanation_es: El caso base está mal: `fib(0)` debe ser `0`, no `1` (solo `fib(1)` es `1`). Con `if n <= 1: return 1` la secuencia se desplaza y `fib(10)` da `89` en vez de `55`. La corrección es distinguir los casos: `if n == 0: return 0` y `if n == 1: return 1` (o `return n if n <= 1 else ...`).
questions.explanation_en: The base case is wrong: `fib(0)` must be `0`, not `1` (only `fib(1)` is `1`). With `if n <= 1: return 1` the whole sequence shifts and `fib(10)` gives `89` instead of `55`. The fix distinguishes the two cases: `if n == 0: return 0` and `if n == 1: return 1` (or `return n if n <= 1 else ...`).
questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Compound statements: Function definitions (recursive calls)

questions.source: CPython docs 3.13 — Data structures: Sets

questions.question_es:
Este código debería imprimir `entrando` y luego `saliendo` usando un context manager propio, pero le falta el método `__exit__`. Corrígelo.

```python
print("saliendo")
```

```python
    def __enter__(self):
        print("entrando")
        return self

with MiContexto():
    pass
print("saliendo")
```
questions.explanation_es: Un context manager (para usarse con `with`) debe implementar tanto `__enter__` como `__exit__`; sin `__exit__` el `with` lanza `AttributeError` al intentar cerrarlo. La corrección añade `def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb): return False` a la clase, que se ejecuta siempre al salir del bloque `with` (incluso si hay excepción).
questions.explanation_en: A context manager (for use with `with`) must implement both `__enter__` and `__exit__`; without `__exit__` the `with` statement raises `AttributeError` when trying to close it. The fix adds `def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb): return False` to the class, which always runs on exiting the `with` block (even if an exception occurred).

questions.explanation_en: `itertools.chain(*iterables)` chains several iterables into one, walking through them in sequence without building an intermediate list. `*anidada` unpacks each sublist as an independent iterable, giving `[1, 2, 3]`.
